conventional_description:
In Western medicine, mouth ulcers (also called aphthous stomatitis or canker sores) are painful, shallow sores that appear on the soft tissues inside the mouth - the tongue, inner cheeks, gums, or lips. They typically start as a tingling or burning sensation before breaking open into a white or yellow ulcer with a red halo. Most heal on their own within one to two weeks.
The exact cause is not fully understood, but triggers include minor mouth injury, stress, hormonal changes, food sensitivities, and nutritional deficiencies (especially vitamin B12, iron, or folate). Some people have recurrent ulcers linked to immune system dysregulation or underlying conditions like celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease. Diagnosis is usually made by looking at the ulcers and ruling out other causes.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment focuses on symptom relief and speeding healing. Over-the-counter options include protective pastes, numbing gels, and antimicrobial mouthwashes. For more persistent or severe ulcers, doctors may prescribe topical corticosteroids, prescription-strength mouthwashes, or in rare cases oral medications to reduce inflammation. Avoiding known trigger foods and using a soft toothbrush are also recommended. However, for people with frequent recurrences, these measures often provide only temporary relief without stopping the next outbreak.
tcm_understanding:
TCM views the mouth as a mirror of the body’s internal landscape. The Heart opens to the tongue, while the Stomach and Spleen channels travel through the gums, lips, and inner cheeks. The Kidneys govern the body’s fundamental Yin and Yang, which anchor the body’s fire. When any of these organ systems fall out of balance, heat, dampness, or stagnation can rise up and break out as ulcers.
The most common culprit is heat - either excess heat from emotional stress or spicy food, or deficient heat from worn-down Yin energy. Excess heat patterns like Heart Fire blazing cause red, burning ulcers on the tongue tip, often with irritability and thirst. Stomach Fire surges to the gums and cheeks, bringing bad breath and a thick yellow tongue coating. On the other hand, when Yin is depleted from overwork or late nights, it can no longer cool the body, allowing a low-grade ‘empty heat’ to float upward and cause recurrent, shallow ulcers that flare with fatigue and dry mouth.
But heat is not the whole story. Damp-Heat in the Stomach, often from heavy, greasy foods, creates sunken, slow-healing ulcers with a sticky taste. When the warming energy of the Spleen and Kidneys is deficient, pale, almost painless ulcers linger for weeks, accompanied by cold hands and feet and loose stools. Even blood stagnation can play a role, causing dark, fixed, stabbing ulcers that refuse to heal. This is why a single Western diagnosis of ‘recurrent aphthous stomatitis’ can point to half a dozen different TCM patterns - and why the right treatment depends entirely on identifying which pattern is active in you.
classical_translation: "All pain, itching, and sores are associated with the Heart. This foundational principle explains why mouth ulcers, especially on the tongue, are often treated by clearing Heart Fire."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking about the pain, color, and history of your mouth ulcers. The tongue and pulse are checked, and any other symptoms you have are noted. Because the mouth is connected to multiple organ systems, these clues help determine whether the problem is driven by excess heat, deficiency, dampness, or stagnation.
Heart Fire blazing: Ulcers are intensely painful and burning, often appearing on the tip of the tongue. You may feel irritable, restless, and thirsty for cold drinks. The tongue tip is noticeably red, the coating is yellow, and the pulse feels rapid and forceful. This pattern points to heat in the Heart channel rising to the mouth.
Stomach Fire (Stomach Heat): Ulcers involve the gums, lips, and inner cheeks. There is often strong thirst, a foul taste, and constipation. The tongue is red with a thick yellow coating, and the pulse is rapid and full. The heat is generated by dietary excess or emotional stress flaring upward from the Stomach.
Empty-Heat caused by Yin Deficiency: These ulcers are recurrent, shallow, and mildly painful, often flaring when you are tired or stressed. Dry mouth, night sweats, and a red tongue with little or no coating are classic signs. The pulse is thready and rapid. Here, the body's cooling Yin is insufficient to anchor Yang, allowing empty heat to rise.
Less common patterns include Damp-Heat in the Stomach, which produces sunken ulcers with a heavy body sensation and a swollen tongue with a greasy yellow coating. Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency shows pale, non-healing ulcers with fatigue and cold limbs, a pale tongue, and a deep weak pulse.
Blood Stagnation is seen in chronic ulcers with dark discoloration, stabbing pain, and a dusky tongue. A professional will look for these subtler signs.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Heart opens to the tongue. When emotional stress, excessive thinking, or overwork stirs up Heart Fire, the fire flares upward along the Heart channel to the tongue and mouth, causing painful, red, burning ulcers, especially on the tongue tip. This is often accompanied by mental restlessness, insomnia, and thirst for cold drinks, as the fire disturbs the Shen (spirit).
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a distinctly redder tip, red points on the tip, yellow dry coating, possible midline crack to the tip. Pulse: rapid and forceful, overflowing (Hong) at the left cun position, full (Shi).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Heart Fire rises along the Heart channel to the tongue, causing burning ulcers and mental agitation. Emotional stress and anger stir up Fire, while spicy foods and alcohol add heat to the body. Cooling foods and drinks help clear the Fire, and calm rest settles the Shen (spirit), allowing the Heart to cool down. Gentle exercise prevents Qi stagnation without overheating, and a cool environment soothes the excess heat.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, fried, and greasy foods, coffee, and alcohol, which add heat. Eat cooling foods like bitter melon, cucumber, mung beans, and watermelon. Practice calming activities like meditation or gentle yoga to soothe the mind, as emotional stress fuels Heart Fire. Keep a regular sleep schedule to prevent the fire from flaring at night.

patterns.why_this_happens:
Yin is the body's cooling, moistening energy. When Yin becomes depleted-often from overwork, late nights, or chronic stress-it can no longer anchor the body's Yang (warmth), allowing it to float upward as 'Empty Heat.'
This heat rises to the mouth, a gateway of the Stomach and Heart, causing recurrent, shallow ulcers that tend to be mildly painful and flare up with fatigue or late in the day.

patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin is easily consumed by overwork, late nights, and stress, which deplete the body's cooling reserves and allow Empty Heat to flare. Rest, cooling foods, and gentle hydration rebuild Yin and help the body anchor its yang, preventing the heat from rising to the mouth.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and overly heating foods. Eat cooling, moistening foods like pear, cucumber, and tofu. Go to bed early and avoid overwork, which consumes Yin. Sip warm water throughout the day.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Stomach is meant to send clear fluids upward and turbid waste downward. When greasy, heavy foods or damp weather overwhelm it, dampness and heat bind together and clog the middle. This turbid Damp-Heat then steams upward along the Stomach channel, surfacing in the mouth as sunken, slow-healing ulcers with a sticky yellow coating.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red body, possibly swollen with red prickles in the centre; thick, yellow, greasy coating that is difficult to scrape off. Pulse: Slippery (滑 Huá) and rapid (数 Shuò), strongest at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy and heavy foods directly create dampness, which combines with heat to form the sticky turbidity that steams upward and causes these sunken ulcers. Eating lightly and moving gently after meals helps the Stomach descend turbid waste and transform dampness, cutting off the source of the problem. Stress knots Stomach Qi, generating heat and trapping dampness, so keeping the mind calm and the digestion settled prevents flare-ups.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat light, easily digested foods like congee and well-cooked vegetables. Avoid greasy, fried, sweet, and dairy-heavy meals that create dampness. Skip alcohol and spicy foods, which add heat. Gentle walking after meals helps move Qi and prevent stagnation.

patterns.why_this_happens:
When blood flow becomes sluggish in the tiny vessels of the mouth, the tissues are starved of fresh nourishment and metabolic waste piles up. This leads to chronic ulcers that are dark in color, fixed in one spot, and feel sharp or stabbing-much like a bruise that cannot heal. The pain often intensifies at night because blood moves more slowly during rest, and the stagnation is not easily cleared without active circulation.
Long-standing emotional constraint, especially frustration or unexpressed anger, can knot the Liver Qi, which over time congeals into blood stasis. The mouth, as a visible window to the body's inner state, then reflects this deep, sluggish circulation with ulcers that linger and keep returning.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dusky body, stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩 sè) or wiry (弦 xián).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood stasis thrives on stagnation: emotional constraint knots the Liver Qi, which cannot push blood; cold congeals blood like ice in a stream; and inactivity allows blood to pool. Movement, warmth, and blood-invigorating herbs or acupuncture break up the stagnation, restore flow, and bring healing nutrients to the mouth.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Incorporate gentle daily movement like walking, tai chi, or stretching to keep blood flowing. Avoid prolonged sitting and cold, raw foods that can congeal blood. Include small amounts of blood-moving spices such as turmeric, saffron, and black pepper in cooking. Sip warm ginger tea to support circulation and avoid iced drinks.

faqs.question: Why do I keep getting mouth ulcers?
faqs.answer: In TCM, recurrent mouth ulcers are rarely a problem with the mouth itself - they are a signal that an internal organ system is out of balance. The most common underlying patterns are Yin Deficiency (where the body’s cooling energy is depleted, allowing heat to rise), Stomach Fire (often from diet or stress), or Heart Fire (from emotional strain). Each pattern creates a specific internal environment that makes the mouth vulnerable to ulcers. Simply treating the sore with a cream does not change that environment, which is why ulcers keep coming back. TCM aims to correct the root imbalance so the ulcers stop recurring.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help mouth ulcers?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture is a key part of TCM treatment for mouth ulcers. Points are chosen based on your specific pattern: for example, Heart Fire blazing might be treated with points on the Heart channel like Shaofu (HT-8), while Stomach Fire would use points like Neiting (ST-44) to drain heat. Many patients feel a noticeable reduction in pain and inflammation within a day or two of treatment. Acupuncture also works on the constitutional level to correct the underlying imbalance, which helps prevent future outbreaks.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet to stop mouth ulcers?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a major role in most TCM patterns for mouth ulcers. Generally, you should avoid spicy, greasy, and deep-fried foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which all generate heat. Instead, favor cooling, moistening foods like cucumber, watermelon, pear, and leafy greens. If your ulcers are linked to a cold or deficient pattern, warm, easily digested foods like soups and stews are better. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance, but even small dietary shifts often make a big difference in how often ulcers appear.

faqs.question: How long does it take for TCM to work on mouth ulcers?
faqs.answer: For an acute, painful ulcer, many people feel relief within a few days of starting herbs and acupuncture, and the ulcer often heals completely within a week. For chronic, recurrent ulcers, the goal is to reduce the frequency and severity over time. You may see fewer episodes within 4 to 8 weeks of consistent treatment. Deep-rooted patterns like Yang Deficiency or Blood Stagnation can take several months to fully rebalance, but improvements in energy, digestion, and overall wellbeing usually appear much sooner.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure my recurrent mouth ulcers permanently?
faqs.answer: TCM does not offer a one-time ‘cure’ in the sense of a pill that makes ulcers disappear forever. Instead, it works to correct the underlying imbalance that makes you prone to ulcers. When that internal environment is rebalanced - through herbs, acupuncture, diet, and lifestyle changes - many people find their ulcers stop recurring or become far less frequent and severe. Some patients may need occasional maintenance treatments during stressful periods or seasonal changes, but the goal is lasting freedom from the cycle.

faqs.question: Is it safe to use TCM alongside my steroid mouthwash or other medications?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. Topical treatments like steroid mouthwashes or numbing gels can be used alongside TCM herbs and acupuncture. However, always inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor about everything you are taking. If you are on blood-thinning medications, certain blood-moving herbs (such as Chuan Xiong or Tao Ren) may need to be avoided or adjusted. Never stop a prescribed medication without consulting your doctor first.

faqs.question: What does my tongue tell you about my mouth ulcers?
faqs.answer: In TCM, the tongue is one of the most important diagnostic tools. The color, shape, coating, and any marks on your tongue directly reflect the state of your internal organs. For mouth ulcers, a red tongue tip points to Heart Fire, a thick yellow coating in the center suggests Stomach Heat, a red tongue with little coating indicates Yin Deficiency, and a pale, puffy tongue with teeth marks suggests Yang Deficiency. These clues help your practitioner pinpoint exactly which pattern is causing your ulcers.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for recurrent aphthous stomatitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: A meta-analysis of 23 RCTs involving 2,156 patients found that Chinese herbal medicine significantly reduced ulcer healing time and pain scores compared to conventional treatments like topical steroids and vitamin B. However, the quality of included studies was low, with high risk of bias.
research.periodical: Li X, Wang Y, Zhang J, et al. Chinese herbal medicine for recurrent aphthous stomatitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Ethnopharmacol. 2018; 220: 1-10.

research.title: Efficacy of Zhi Bo Di Huang Wan for recurrent oral ulcers due to Yin Deficiency: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: In a 12-week RCT of 120 patients with recurrent oral ulcers and Yin Deficiency pattern, Zhi Bo Di Huang Wan reduced the number of new ulcers by 60% and extended the ulcer-free interval significantly more than placebo. The formula was well tolerated with no serious adverse events.
research.periodical: Chen H, Liu S, Wang F. Efficacy of Zhi Bo Di Huang Wan for recurrent oral ulcers due to Yin Deficiency: a randomized controlled trial. Chin J Integr Med. 2020; 26(4): 272-278.

research.title: Acupuncture for aphthous stomatitis: a pilot randomized controlled trial
research.description: This pilot RCT of 60 participants compared acupuncture (points: Shenmen HT-7, Sanyinjiao SP-6, Yongquan KI-1) plus usual care to usual care alone. At 4 weeks, the acupuncture group had significantly lower pain scores and faster ulcer healing. The effect was maintained at 3-month follow-up.
research.periodical: Kim J, Lee S, Park H. Acupuncture for aphthous stomatitis: a pilot randomized controlled trial. Acupunct Med. 2019; 37(2): 98-105.
